title: What gospel did Jesus preach?
question: When Jesus went around 'preaching the gospel', what exactly was the good news he announced, and how do scholars disagree about it?
plainAnswer: Jesus' good news was that God was at last becoming king, as Israel's prophets had promised, and that this reign was breaking in through him. He called people to turn around (repent), trust this news, and follow him. He showed what the kingdom looked like by healing the sick, freeing the oppressed, eating with outsiders and forgiving sinners, and he explained it in parables. As his ministry went on he said plainly that he must suffer, die and rise, and he gave that death a saving meaning at the Last Supper. Scholars agree that 'the kingdom of God' was the centre of his message; they disagree about whether he thought of it as mostly present, mostly future, or both at once.
keyTakeaways: Jesus' headline was 'the kingdom of God has come near' (Mark 1:15), not a general invitation to go to heaven when you die.
'Kingdom of God' means God's active rule or reign more than a place; it draws on Isaiah's herald of good news and Daniel's vision of the Son of Man.
Healings, exorcisms and table fellowship with sinners were presented as signs that the reign of God was already arriving.
Jesus did warn of judgment, including Gehenna, and did promise life in the age to come; these sit inside the kingdom message rather than replacing it.
He predicted his death and resurrection and interpreted his death as a ransom and covenant sacrifice, which links his preaching to the apostles' later preaching about him.
The main scholarly debate is timing: future and imminent (Weiss, Schweitzer), already fully present (Dodd), or already and not yet (Ladd, Meier, Dunn, Wright and most today).

sections.heading: The headline: God's kingdom has come near
sections.body:
Mark sums up Jesus' preaching in one sentence: the time is fulfilled, the kingdom of God has come near, repent and believe the good news (Mark 1:14-15). Matthew describes him going through Galilee 'preaching the gospel of the kingdom' and healing every disease (Matt 4:23; Matt 9:35). Luke has Jesus say that he must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to other towns too, 'for this is why I was sent' (Luke 4:43).

The word 'gospel' (Greek *euangelion*) simply means good news, especially news of a victory or a new ruler. In the Roman world it was used of the birth and accession of emperors; a famous inscription from Priene in Asia Minor (9 BC) calls Augustus' birthday the beginning of good news for the world. Jesus' hearers, though, would have heard the word mainly through Isaiah, where a messenger runs to Jerusalem with news that 'your God reigns' (Isa 52:7; Isa 40:9).

So the gospel Jesus preached was first of all an announcement about God, not a technique for individuals. The fitting response was to repent (change direction) and believe (trust and commit to) the news.

callout.text: Myth: 'the gospel of the kingdom' and 'the gospel of grace' are two different gospels. Some dispensational writers have drawn this distinction, but most interpreters across traditions see one gospel: Jesus announced the kingdom, and the apostles announced the same kingdom now opened through his death and resurrection (Acts 8:12; Acts 28:31).

sections.heading: Old Testament roots: Isaiah's herald, Isaiah 61 and Daniel 7
sections.body:
Jesus did not invent the idea of God's kingdom. Israel already sang that the Lord is king, and the prophets looked forward to a day when God would act decisively to rescue his people, deal with evil and rule over all nations (Isa 52:7-10; Mic 4:1-4; Zech 14:9).

In Nazareth, Luke says, Jesus read Isaiah 61: the Spirit of the Lord has anointed me to bring good news to the poor, release to captives, sight to the blind and freedom to the oppressed, and to proclaim the year of the Lord's favour. Then he said, 'Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing' (Luke 4:16-21; Isa 61:1-2). 'The year of the Lord's favour' echoes the Jubilee, when debts were cancelled and land returned (Lev 25:8-12).

Daniel 7 supplies the other key picture. After a series of beast-like empires, 'one like a son of man' comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion, which is then shared with the holy people of the Most High (Dan 7:13-14; Dan 7:27). Jesus' favourite self-description, 'the Son of Man', and his answer at his trial (Mark 14:61-62) tie his mission to this vision of God's kingdom replacing the empires.

callout.text: Luke quotes Isaiah 61:1-2 but stops before 'and the day of vengeance of our God'. Many readers see this as deliberate: the present phase of Jesus' ministry is favour and release, with judgment still to come. Others think too much is made of where a reading ended.

sections.heading: What 'the kingdom of God' meant
sections.body:
In the Gospels 'kingdom' (Greek *basileia*) usually means God's reign, his rule in action, rather than a territory or a place in the sky. Matthew mostly says 'kingdom of heaven', following the Jewish habit of reverently avoiding the word God; it means the same thing as 'kingdom of God' in Mark and Luke (compare Matt 19:23-24).

The kingdom is something people can enter, receive like children, seek first, inherit and pray for (Mark 10:15; Matt 6:33; Matt 25:34). The Lord's Prayer defines it by parallel: your kingdom come, your will be done on earth as in heaven (Matt 6:10). So the hope is that heaven's rule comes to earth, not that people leave earth for heaven.

At the same time it has an end-time side. Many will come from east and west to feast with Abraham in the kingdom (Matt 8:11-12), the Twelve will judge Israel's tribes in the renewal of all things (Matt 19:28), and Jesus will not drink wine again until he drinks it new in the kingdom (Mark 14:25).

sections.heading: Parables: the kingdom told in stories
sections.body:
Jesus explained the kingdom mainly through parables, short stories drawn from farming, households, money and feasts. Several make the same surprising point: the kingdom starts small and hidden but grows to fill everything, like a mustard seed or yeast in dough (Mark 4:30-32; Matt 13:33), or seed that grows while the farmer sleeps (Mark 4:26-29).

Other parables stress its worth and the response it demands: the hidden treasure and the pearl worth selling everything for (Matt 13:44-46). Some warn that the good and bad will be sorted only at the end (Matt 13:24-30; Matt 13:47-50). The great banquet shows the poor, the crippled and outsiders filling the places that invited guests refused (Luke 14:15-24). The lost sheep, coin and son show God's joy over one sinner who repents (Luke 15).

Jesus also said parables both reveal and conceal: they open the kingdom to those willing to hear and leave the hard-hearted puzzled (Mark 4:10-12). They invite the hearer to make a judgment and so to take a side.

sections.heading: Healings, exorcisms and meals as signs
sections.body:
When John the Baptist, in prison, sent to ask whether Jesus was the one to come, Jesus pointed to what was happening: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised and the poor have good news preached to them (Matt 11:2-6). These phrases echo Isaiah's pictures of God's coming rescue (Isa 35:5-6; Isa 61:1).

He treated exorcisms the same way: if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you (Luke 11:20; Matt 12:28). The strong man is being tied up and his house plundered (Mark 3:27). When he sent out the Twelve and the seventy-two, their instructions were to heal and to say that the kingdom had come near (Matt 10:7-8; Luke 10:9).

His meals mattered too. Eating with tax collectors and sinners was a public sign that God was welcoming the lost back (Mark 2:15-17; Luke 15:1-2). Almost all historians, including sceptical ones, accept that Jesus was known as a healer and exorcist; they differ about how to explain the reports.

sections.heading: Forgiveness, repentance and the call to follow
sections.body:
Jesus announced forgiveness directly, which shocked his critics: 'Son, your sins are forgiven', followed by healing as proof that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive (Mark 2:1-12). He told a sinful woman that her faith had saved her (Luke 7:36-50) and declared that salvation had come to Zacchaeus' house (Luke 19:1-10).

The welcome came with a demand. Repent, he said, or you will all likewise perish (Luke 13:3-5). He called disciples to deny themselves, take up their cross and follow him (Mark 8:34-38), and told a rich man to sell everything and follow (Mark 10:17-31). The Sermon on the Mount describes the kind of life the kingdom produces: blessing on the poor, the mourning and the persecuted, love of enemies, secret piety and trust in the Father (Matt 5:3-12; Matt 5:43-48; Matt 6:25-34).

In plain terms, grace and demand were not opposites in his preaching. The undeserved welcome was the reason for the costly change.

sections.heading: Judgment, Gehenna and the life of the age to come
sections.body:
It would be wrong to say Jesus never spoke about what happens after death. He warned of Gehenna, usually translated hell, more than anyone else in the New Testament (Matt 5:22; Matt 10:28; Mark 9:43-48). He spoke of a final separation of sheep and goats (Matt 25:31-46) and of the rich man in Hades (Luke 16:19-31). He promised 'eternal life', which in the Synoptic Gospels means the life of the age to come, the same as entering the kingdom (Mark 10:17; Mark 10:23-30).

But these warnings sit inside the kingdom message. Judgment is the other side of God putting the world right. Jesus' sharpest warnings were often aimed at the religious and the comfortable, not at outsiders (Matt 23:33; Luke 6:24-26).

How to read Gehenna (eternal conscious punishment, final destruction, or a purifying judgment) is a separate debate covered elsewhere in the app.

callout.text: Two opposite myths: that Jesus never mentioned hell (he did, often), and that his gospel was basically about escaping hell (his headline was the arrival of God's reign, with judgment as part of it). Both oversimplify the texts.

sections.heading: The cross and resurrection in Jesus' own preaching
sections.body:
From Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi onward, Mark records three explicit predictions: the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed and after three days rise (Mark 8:31; Mark 9:31; Mark 10:33-34). He then gives the reason: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45), language that echoes the suffering servant of Isaiah (Isa 53:10-12).

At the Last Supper he interpreted his coming death as covenant blood poured out for many, and Matthew adds 'for the forgiveness of sins' (Mark 14:22-25; Matt 26:28). After the resurrection Luke presents Jesus teaching that the scriptures foretold the Messiah's suffering and rising and that repentance for forgiveness should be preached to all nations in his name (Luke 24:46-47).

Historians debate how much of the predictions' precise wording comes from Jesus and how much was sharpened after Easter. Most agree that Jesus expected a violent death and gave it meaning in advance, especially at the Last Supper.

sections.heading: How scholars differ: present, future, or both?
sections.body:
Johannes Weiss (1892) and Albert Schweitzer (*The Quest of the Historical Jesus*, German original 1906) argued that Jesus expected the kingdom to arrive very soon as a dramatic, world-ending act of God, and that he died trying to force its coming. This is called 'consistent' or 'thoroughgoing' eschatology. Texts like Mark 9:1 and Mark 13:30 are their strongest evidence.

C. H. Dodd (*The Parables of the Kingdom*, 1935) swung the other way with 'realised eschatology': in Jesus' ministry the kingdom had fully arrived; Luke 11:20 and Luke 17:20-21 were key. George Eldon Ladd (*The Presence of the Future*, 1974) and many others argued for 'inaugurated eschatology': the kingdom is already present in Jesus but not yet complete. This already-and-not-yet view is now the majority position, held in various forms by Meier, Dunn and Wright, and Dodd himself later moved somewhat toward it.

E. P. Sanders (*Jesus and Judaism*, 1985) placed Jesus within 'restoration eschatology': he expected God to restore Israel (the Twelve symbolising the tribes, the temple action pointing to a new temple). N. T. Wright (*Jesus and the Victory of God*, 1996) argued that Jesus announced the end of Israel's long exile and God's return to Zion, embodied in his own journey to Jerusalem and death.

callout.text: Luke 17:21 can be translated 'the kingdom of God is within you' (KJV) or 'among you / in your midst' (most modern versions). The first suggests an inner spiritual reality; the second points to Jesus' own presence. Most scholars prefer 'among you', since Jesus is addressing Pharisees, but the inward reading has a long history.

timeline.title: Jesus begins preaching in Galilee
timeline.note: After John's arrest, Jesus announces that the kingdom has come near (Mark 1:14-15). Exact year debated (27-29).

timeline.title: Parables and the mission of the Twelve
timeline.note: Jesus teaches in parables and sends the Twelve to preach the kingdom and heal.

timeline.title: Caesarea Philippi and the passion predictions
timeline.note: After Peter's confession, Jesus begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer and rise.

timeline.title: Last Supper, crucifixion and resurrection
timeline.note: Jesus interprets his death as covenant blood; crucified under Pilate, most likely in AD 30 or 33.

timeline.title: Johannes Weiss on the kingdom
timeline.note: Argues the kingdom in Jesus' preaching was future and apocalyptic.

timeline.title: Dodd's realised eschatology
timeline.note: *The Parables of the Kingdom* argues the kingdom had arrived in Jesus.

timeline.title: Ladd's inaugurated kingdom
timeline.note: *The Presence of the Future* popularises the already-and-not-yet view.

timeline.title: Wright's Jesus and the Victory of God
timeline.note: Reads Jesus' message as the end of exile and the return of Israel's God to Zion.

views.name: Consistent (future) eschatology
views.summary: Weiss and Schweitzer: Jesus expected an imminent, dramatic end of the age; the kingdom was wholly future and he was mistaken about its timing. Few scholars hold it in this pure form today, but its stress on Jesus' urgency is widely accepted.

views.name: Realised eschatology
views.summary: Dodd: the kingdom fully arrived in Jesus' ministry, death and resurrection; future language is symbolic of its significance. Valued for highlighting present fulfilment, but criticised for flattening the future sayings.

views.name: Inaugurated (already and not yet)
views.summary: Ladd, Kümmel, Meier, Dunn and most current scholars: God's reign truly began in Jesus but awaits completion at his return. Critics say it can become a way to avoid hard texts about imminence.

views.name: Restoration of Israel
views.summary: Sanders and Wright: Jesus' message centred on God restoring Israel and returning as king, with the nations then blessed. Critics question whether 'continuing exile' was as widespread an idea as Wright claims.

views.name: Moral and spiritual kingdom
views.summary: Older liberal Protestants such as Albrecht Ritschl and Adolf von Harnack (*What Is Christianity?*, 1900) read the kingdom mainly as God's rule in the soul and the ethic of love. Weiss and Schweitzer's work was largely a reaction against this view.
